conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. You're in the hospital because your blood sugar was extremely high when EMS brought you in. Do you remember what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah… I was feeling sick, throwing up. I couldn’t keep anything down, so I didn’t take my insulin. I also had some vodka the night before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. When you’re vomiting and miss insulin, your body can go into diabetic ketoacidosis, or DKA. Your blood sugar was over 1100, and your pH was very low—6.91—which is dangerous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh… I didn’t realize it was that bad. I just felt cold and weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You were also very dehydrated and had a low blood pressure—66 over 35 at one point. We gave you fluids and started an insulin drip to bring things under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember the IV. Was I in danger?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, DKA can be life-threatening. But we caught it early and started treatment right away. You’re responding well. We also gave you sodium bicarbonate because your blood was too acidic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… that’s good. What about my heart? I saw wires when I woke up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an ECG. You had some changes—peaked T waves and ST depressions—which can happen with high potassium or acidosis. But your troponins were normal, so no heart attack. It’s likely due to the DKA.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had high potassium before. Was it bad this time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your potassium was 7.4, which is very high. We treated it with insulin and calcium to protect your heart. As your blood sugar comes down, your potassium is improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my kidneys? Last time I was here, my creatinine went up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine was elevated to 1.7, but that’s due to dehydration from high glucose. We call it pre-renal azotemia. With fluids, it’s already improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been trying to manage my diabetes better, but when I get sick, it’s hard.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s completely understandable. Illness and vomiting make it tough. But missing insulin, especially with alcohol, increases your risk of DKA.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know… I’ve been working on my drinking. I went to a few outpatient sessions after last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. We’ll make sure you’re connected with support again before discharge. Your mental health and substance use are just as important as your diabetes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are improving. Your glucose is down to 250, and your bicarbonate is up to 18. The acidosis is resolving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Can I eat something? I’m feeling a little better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start you on clear liquids. Once you can keep food down, we’ll transition you back to subcutaneous insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I go back to my usual insulin dose?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Actually, the endocrinology team reviewed your case. They recommend increasing your bedtime Lantus from 5 to 8 units to help prevent future DKA episodes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I can do that. I just don’t want to end up back here again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll help you avoid that. We’ll go over sick-day rules—when to check ketones, how to adjust insulin, and when to seek help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We placed a venous catheter in your leg to make it easier to give fluids and medications. It’s temporary and will be removed before you go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s a little uncomfortable, but I understand. Is everything else okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your chest X-ray showed mild congestion, but no pneumonia. Your lungs are clear, and you’re breathing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that before—probably from being dehydrated. My blood pressure was low earlier, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you had shock from the DKA. We gave you a medication called levophed to support your blood pressure. It’s been weaned off, and your BP is stable now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad it’s better. I was scared when I couldn’t stand up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re through the worst of it. Your repeat ECG looks better too—no new changes. Your potassium is now 4.6, which is normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood count? I’ve been anemic before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin is 10.0, which is low but stable. It’s likely chronic from your diabetes and other factors. We’ll continue your iron and follow it as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. You’ve been eating, your glucose is stable, and your labs are nearly normal. We’re switching you fully to subcutaneous insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Can I walk around a bit more?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. We encourage you to stay active. Your strength is returning, and you’re no longer on bed rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been thinking about my drinking. I want to go back to counseling. Can you help me set that up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll connect you with the addiction medicine team today. They’ll help you schedule outpatient rehab and support groups.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I know it’s part of why I keep getting sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re taking the right steps. Managing both diabetes and alcohol use is hard, but you’re not alone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs this morning are excellent. Glucose is 180, bicarbonate is 22, and creatinine is back to 0.6. You’re ready for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What do I need to do when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue your medications, especially the increased Lantus dose. Check your blood sugar regularly and test for ketones if you’re sick or over 250.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I start vomiting again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Try to sip water and take half your usual insulin dose. If you can’t keep fluids down or your ketones are high, come to the ER right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see your primary care doctor and endocrinologist in one week. We’ve scheduled your rehab intake for next Monday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I really appreciate the help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home. Your vitals are stable, and you’re feeling well. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just one—should I restart my blood pressure meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve restarted lisinopril and metoprolol. They were held during your low blood pressure but are safe now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my depression meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue venlafaxine and mirtazapine. Mental health is key—don’t skip those.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I won’t. I’m going to try harder this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s all we ask. You’re going home in good shape. Take care of yourself, and we’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I’ll follow up with everyone.
